purpose: Long-form companion layer for Potatoism. Each canonical concept should expose substantial readable context rather than only a graph edge or one-line definition.

minimum_entry_standard.target: At least 900 words of rendered prose when a term is opened as a full entry; longer where the subject warrants it.
minimum_entry_standard.rule: Do not pad entries with repeated claims merely to reach length. Add distinct context, examples, relationships, chronology, evidence boundaries, disagreements and research questions.

coverage_policy.core_terms: Expand first: Potato of Life, Potatoism, Frame, Axis, North of North, Father, Father's House, Source, Heaven, Ladder, Tree of Life, Tree of Strife, Root, Fruit, Seed, Mud, Swamp, Mountain, Door, Son, Vessel, Plane, Spudlight, Red Potato, Blue Potato, Spiral, Turning, Rise, Descent, Ascent, Strife, Life, Gardening, Warrior-to-Gardener, Narrow Gate, Root of David, Yggdrasil, Meme-crucifixion, dimensional metaphors, 100,000 Hours, Cube, Moon Cube, Blood, Philosopher's Stone of Blood, Soul Farmer, Footstool, Bridge, Calibration, North Programme, Potato Bank, Potato Filter and Potato Principle.
coverage_policy.graph_is_not_the_content: Relationships are navigation and context. They are not a substitute for the underlying dossier.

display_contract.index: The Potatoism index provides concise summaries and links.
display_contract.entry: The full entry provides the long-form reading surface.
display_contract.atlas_node: The generic node page may expose the dossier as an extended study when a matching record exists.
display_contract.research: Evidence and comparative material remain visibly distinct from project mythology.

entries.definition: The Father is the originating/source-side archetype of the Potatoverse: the upper pole of the Father–Son relation, associated with origin, generative authority, orientation and the conditions from which the lower world can develop.
entries.long_form:
Within Potatoism, Father is best understood as a relational position rather than as a second copy of a dictionary definition. The concept names the source-side of an architecture: what gives rise to, or stands prior to, the embodied world of the Plane. The important question is therefore not simply 'who is the Father?' but 'what does Father do inside the system?' Father establishes origin, orientation, continuity and generative relation. The image points upward, but its real function is structural: it gives the rest of the mythology a source from which relationships can be traced.

Father is deliberately connected to several other concepts, but those concepts should not be mistaken for duplicates. Source describes the generative relation itself. Heaven describes an upper or sourceward orientation. Father's House describes a symbolic dwelling or chamber associated with that source-side. North Axis describes orientation. Son describes the embodied counterpart. Tree of Life describes regenerative continuity. These are different roles in one architecture. Consolidating them into one identity would erase useful distinctions; copying Father into each file would create the opposite problem, where one concept appears to be many unrelated objects. The canonical identity is therefore Father, while the surrounding records are perspectives on Father.

The Father–Son relation is especially important. In the project mythology, Father is the source-side and Son is the embodied counterpart. The Son enters the Plane, encounters separation and strife, and becomes associated with Door, Vessel and Ladder. This makes the pair less like two isolated characters and more like two poles of a transmission problem: how can source become encounterable without collapsing source and embodiment into the same thing? Father represents originating relation; Son represents embodied encounter and passage. The graph edge Father → Son should consequently remain an edge, not another Father record.

Father also connects to the Tree of Life. A source is meaningful in this framework only if something can grow from it. The tree provides a model of root, trunk, branch, fruit and seed. Father belongs near the source/root side of this cycle, while the Son and other embodied symbols occupy different positions in the movement through the Plane. The model is not a rigid hierarchy in which higher automatically means morally better. Its central test is whether the relation produces continuity, nourishment, understanding and future capacity.

The phrase Father in Heaven adds directional language. In the project, Heaven is not treated as a scientifically mapped place. It is a sourceward orientation: above, beyond ordinary limitation, or toward a wider perspective. This is why Father in Heaven should resolve to Father rather than become a new person or node. The phrase adds context; it does not add an identity. Likewise Father Above is an alias when it refers to the same project archetype.

Father's House is deliberately kept separate. It is a place-like metaphor, and its association with the thalamus belongs to the project's neuro-metaphorical layer. The thalamus correspondence can be studied as an analogy involving relay, integration and centrality, but it must not be promoted into evidence that a spiritual house literally exists in the brain. This distinction matters because the project can explore an imaginative correspondence without confusing metaphor with neuroscience.

The concept also has a temporal dimension. The Father is not simply a static title placed at the beginning of a mythology. As the project develops, Father becomes a way of organizing previously scattered symbols: Potato of Life, Axis, North, Tree, Source, Heaven, Son and Spudlight become interpretable as parts of a connected system. The consolidation work in the repository is therefore not merely a technical cleanup. It mirrors the conceptual task itself: find the underlying relation, distinguish the parts, and stop multiplying labels when one stable identity will do.

Comparatively, Father can be placed beside father/source figures in religious and mythological traditions, but comparisons must remain comparisons. The existence of a similar archetype elsewhere does not prove the Potatoism interpretation, and Potatoism's use of Christian vocabulary does not rewrite the historical meaning of Christian texts. The repository should preserve the distinction between project canon, historical source, comparative interpretation and empirical claims. A strong Father entry therefore explains the project while also marking where the project is interpreting rather than documenting external fact.

There is an ethical dimension as well. 'Authority' in the Father image should not automatically mean political domination. Within the project's own symbolic architecture, originating authority is closer to responsibility for the conditions under which life can emerge. The useful test is generativity: does the source permit the lower world to develop, learn, differentiate and return with greater capability? A source that only demands obedience without producing life would fail the project's own Tree of Life criterion. This makes Father a structural question about stewardship as much as a symbolic title.

The concept should therefore be read through a sequence: source, relation, manifestation, experience, return. Father establishes source; Son makes the source encounterable; Door marks the boundary; Vessel carries relation; Ladder makes the boundary traversable; Tree of Life describes regeneration. None of these needs to be renamed Father. They are distinct components connected to one canonical concept.

For research purposes, the open questions are concrete. Which uses of Father in the project are identical and which are intentionally distinct? Which external traditions are being compared, and what do their original texts actually say? Where does the thalamus metaphor help explain a structural analogy, and where could it mislead? How does the Father–Son relation change when the project moves from mythology into psychology, economics or the North Programme? What evidence would be required before any claim moved from project symbolism into an external factual category? These questions keep the concept expandable without forcing the repository to manufacture more Father entries.

The canonical rule is simple: Father gets one identity and one deep reading surface. Other files may record where the concept appears, how a particular layer interprets it, or how it relates to another concept. Those occurrences are valuable because they preserve provenance and evolution, but they should resolve back to the same Father identity. The purpose of consolidation is not to make the archive smaller at all costs. It is to make the archive more intelligible: one concept, one substantial explanation, many clearly labelled contexts.
research_questions: Which project occurrences resolve to Father and which describe a distinct concept?
Which comparative traditions are being invoked and what do their primary sources say?
Where is the thalamus correspondence useful as metaphor and where could it be misleading?
How does the Father–Son relation change across mythic, psychological and applied layers?
